title: Palantir Revenue Nearly Doubles as AI Demand Drives 'Otherworldly' Quarter
excerpt: The data analytics company reported Q2 revenue of $1.94 billion, up 93% year-over-year, with U.S. commercial sales surging 149% as enterprises race to deploy sovereign AI platforms.
body:
• Palantir reported Q2 revenue of $1.94 billion, up 93% year-over-year, crushing analyst expectations of $1.81 billion
  • U.S. commercial revenue surged 149% to $764 million as enterprises accelerated adoption of sovereign AI platforms
  • The company raised its full-year revenue guidance to $8.15 billion, nearly $500 million above its previous forecast
  • Shares jumped roughly 15% after CEO Alex Karp called the quarter "otherworldly" and took aim at AI labs over token pricing

Palantir Technologies delivered its strongest quarter yet on Monday, reporting revenue that nearly doubled and prompting CEO Alex Karp to describe the results as "otherworldly." The data analytics company posted $1.94 billion in second-quarter revenue, a 93% increase from the same period last year and roughly $130 million above Wall Street consensus estimates.

Adjusted earnings per share hit $0.41, well ahead of the $0.34 analysts had expected and more than triple the $0.13 reported a year ago. Net income reached $1.06 billion, meaning Palantir generated more profit in a single quarter than its entire revenue from the same period in 2025.

U.S. Commercial Sales Power the Surge

The standout number was U.S. commercial revenue, which grew 149% year-over-year to $764 million. U.S. government revenue climbed 90% to $809 million. Together, U.S. operations accounted for 81% of total revenue.

Deal activity hit records across the board. Palantir closed 220 deals worth at least $1 million, including 73 exceeding $10 million. U.S. commercial total contract value bookings reached $2.13 billion, up 153% from a year ago and nearly $800 million above the previous quarterly record.

"Demand for AI sovereignty has now been unleashed. Our customers trust us to provide them with maximal control over their operations, data and decisions."

— Alex Karp, CEO, Palantir Technologies

Taking Aim at AI Labs

Karp used the earnings call to sharpen his criticism of major AI labs, including OpenAI and Anthropic, over their pricing and data practices. He argued that companies using token-based AI services are effectively surrendering their competitive advantages.

"Companies are paying to give away their most important secrets, the very basis for their competitive advantage," said Ryan Taylor, Palantir's chief revenue and chief legal officer. Palantir recently published a white paper titled "Institutional Sovereignty in the Age of AI," outlining 15 steps organisations could take to protect themselves.

The pitch has resonated. William Blair analyst Louie DiPalma said the results shifted the narrative around the stock "from AI loser to AI winner," noting that no other public software company or defence contractor matched Palantir's combination of revenue growth and profitability. He sees upside toward the $200 range over the next year.

Guidance Raises the Bar

Management raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to between $8.15 billion and $8.16 billion, up from a prior forecast under $7.7 billion. U.S. commercial revenue is now expected to exceed $3.42 billion, implying at least 134% full-year growth. For Q3, the company guided for revenue of roughly $2.16 billion, well above estimates of around $2 billion.

Adjusted free cash flow hit a record $1.22 billion, a 63% margin. The company's Rule of 40 score — a software industry metric combining revenue growth and profit margin — reached 155%, its twelfth consecutive quarter of improvement. Palantir ended the quarter with $9.2 billion in cash and virtually no debt.

What to Watch

Shares surged roughly 15% on Tuesday to around $147, putting the stock on track to recover much of its 30% year-to-date decline. But the rally also raised the valuation stakes. Investors will be watching whether U.S. commercial revenue growth can sustain its pace, whether government contracts remain durable under shifting federal priorities, and whether Palantir's sovereign AI thesis can fend off competition from hyperscalers and enterprise software rivals now building their own platforms.

Cantor analysts hiked their price target to $156 from $138 but maintained a Neutral rating, reflecting the tension between exceptional execution and the stock's premium multiple. For investors with exposure to U.S. tech and AI, the quarter was hard to argue with — but so is the price of admission.
